classification_signals: Page 4: 'This publication is one of a series produced as part of WWF-UK's Strategies for Change Project. This project seeks to examine the empirical basis for today's dominant approaches to environmental communications and campaigns, and to ask why these are failing to create the level of change that is needed.'

Page 6 (Foreword): 'The authors have amassed a sophisticated theoretical and empirical case for a fundamental re-evaluation of mainstream approaches to environmental communications and campaigning. Their thinking goes beyond an analysis of the problems of our current approach: it also suggests clear and intriguing new possibilities that hold a great deal of promise.'

Page 8 (Contents): Structured into 'HUMAN IDENTITY AND ENVIRONMENTAL CHALLENGES', 'IDENTITY CAMPAIGNING: STRATEGIES...', 'REASONS TO BE CHEERFUL...', indicating a problem-analysis-solution structure based on existing knowledge.

Page 10 (Introduction): 'Here we present an overview of these two strategies as a prelude to introducing a third approach to which we feel the environmental movement must pay close attention. We believe that this third approach, which we call identity campaigning, holds substantial promise...' This introduces a new conceptual approach.

Page 16 (Part I): 'In Part I we identify three aspects of human identity that empirical research suggests are associated with behavioural decisions that often serve to frustrate optimal responses to environmental challenges.' This confirms the review of empirical research to build a theoretical case.
title: Meeting Environmental Challenges: The Role of Human Identity

limitations: The three aspects of human identity selected for analysis may not constitute a complete list, nor necessarily the most important features of the human psyche involved in frustrating environmental responses (Page 16).
The proposed agenda for shifting values and life goals extends far beyond the current scope of most environmental organisations, posing an implementation challenge (Page 37).

Relatively little theory and research specifically addresses practical responses to prejudice towards non-human nature, and applying techniques from human-human interactions to human-nature relationships is likely to entail specific challenges requiring more work (Page 46).
The proposals for engaging dominant values and aspects of identity are ambitious, and the environmental movement cannot make progress in this way whilst working alone (Page 69).

Implementing the proposed approach requires changes in current monitoring and evaluation processes, as defining campaign success solely by short-term material policy outcomes makes it difficult to integrate cognitive policy goals (Page 72).
minimum_safe_summary: This narrative review by Crompton and Kasser (2009) proposes 'identity campaigning' as a crucial third approach for the environmental movement, arguing that current strategies focusing on engaging organizations and specific behaviors are insufficient. The paper synthesizes empirical and theoretical literature to identify three environmentally problematic aspects of human identity: self-enhancing/materialistic values, in-group/out-group distinctions (anthropocentrism), and maladaptive coping mechanisms for fear and threats. Key findings include that materialistic values are negatively associated with pro-environmental attitudes and behaviors, defining nature as an 'out-group' hinders connection and pro-environmental action, and coping strategies like 'seeking pleasure' or 'denial of guilt' reduce stress but do not promote beneficial environmental behaviors. The authors suggest strategies to mitigate these issues, such as reducing social modeling of materialism, promoting intrinsic values, fostering empathy for non-human nature, and encouraging healthier coping mechanisms like mindfulness. Limitations include the acknowledged incompleteness of the identified identity aspects and the ambitious nature of the proposed interventions, requiring new collaborations and changes in campaign evaluation.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Distinguishes between intrinsic (e.g., community, personal growth) and extrinsic (e.g., money, fame, image) aspirations/values, arguing that intrinsic values are associated with psychological well-being and pro-social/pro-environmental behavior, while extrinsic values are linked to poorer well-being and less pro-social/pro-environmental behavior. The paper applies this framework to understanding environmental challenges.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Schwartz's Theory of Basic Human Values
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Proposes a universal structure of human values, often categorized into higher-order dimensions like self-enhancement (power, achievement) vs. self-transcendence (universalism, benevolence). The paper uses this distinction to explain how certain value orientations (e.g., self-enhancement/materialism) undermine environmental concern, while others (e.g., self-transcendence) promote it.

Different forms of identity (e.g., personal, social, ecological) and their salience influence how individuals perceive environmental issues and their motivation to act. The paper argues for fostering identities that are more inclusive and connected to nature.

instruments_used.name: Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ)
instruments_used.description: Self-report questionnaire measuring individual value priorities based on Schwartz's theory, typically using short portraits of people.

instruments_used.name: New Ecological Paradigm Scale (NEP)
instruments_used.description: Measures an individual's endorsement of an ecological worldview, often used to assess pro-environmental attitudes.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper proposes that strong endorsement of self-enhancing, materialistic values leads individuals to prioritize personal gain and consumption, fostering an instrumental view of nature as a resource rather than something to be protected. This instrumental view, in turn, results in less positive attitudes towards non-human nature.
